newsitem.title: THAILAND: Japan cautiously awaits Thai-IMF package.
newsitem.headline: Japan cautiously awaits Thai-IMF package.

text.p: Japanese bankers said on Tuesday they were waiting to see how Thailand would restructure its economy before making any decisions on a planned rescue package.

Officials of the Export-Import Bank (Ex-Im) Bank of Japan and private Japanese banks, widely expected to come up with billions of dollars in loans to Thailand, said they were paying special attention to how Bangkok bailed out its financial sector, saddled with mountains of "bubble era" debts.

"Everything is still up in the air, it all depends on the shape of likely agreement with the Thai government and the IMF (International Monetary Fund) on the economic package," an official at the Ex-Im bank in Bangkok told Reuters when asked about possible bank loans to Thailand.
The official at the government entity said the body could not lend money to bail out bad loans in Thailand's private finance sector.

"We are keeping a close watch on how Thailand will deal with massive bad loans held by the Thai financial sector," the official said. "We must avoid letting our money be used to dispose of private-sector bad loans of any other nations."
Earlier in Tokyo, Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said that Japan would come up with the necessary steps to help Thailand's economy once Bangkok and the IMF reached final agreement.
An international monetary source in Tokyo played down any imminent prospect of Japan announcing its rescue steps until actual figures were announced by Thailand.
Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya was expected to present the package later on Tuesday after winning cabinet approval.
Japanese officials have said that Tokyo's rescue measures for Bangkok, consisting mainly of untied loans from the Ex-Im Bank of Japan, will be in place within next two weeks.

A Japanese daily, the Yomiuri Shimbun, reported on Tuesday that the IMF, the Asian Development Bank, Japan's Ex-Im Bank and Japanese commercial banks would provide a total of $10 billion to help get Thailand's economy back on its feet.
The Thai economy is growing at its slowest pace in a decade amid slowing exports and a liquidity crunch in the financial sector, which is already over-exposed to the property market.
The economic crisis, which threatened to bankrupt Thailand's financial sector, forced the government and the business community to swallow national pride and seek IMF help.

Nobuo Nakayama, joint general manager of Sakura Bank Ltd in Bangkok, said it was reasonable for Japan to take the initiative in crafting rescue steps, given its heavy loan exposure to the country as well as hefty direct investment by Japanese firms.

"I think Japan will be greatly involved in a rescue package, and the reality is moving in this direction," he said. But he added it would be difficult to decide on any emergency loans unless Thailand specified how much money was needed to solve which particular kind of problems.
Thailand has nearly $90 billion in foreign currency debt, and Japanese bankers estimate about $36 billion of that is owed to Japanese banks.
Doubts also linger over whether Japanese banks, whose financial strength has deteriorated as a result of their own bad loan woes, can form a united front in making syndicate loans.

"Some banks, which have already extended loans to any of the 16 ailing Thai finance firms (which have suspended business since June) could be more cautious in making additional loans to Thailand," said Nakayama.
"Each bank should make its own decision...but, in general, some banks could say that they would refrain from participating in (the rescue loans)," he said.
